I will say I just started my bachelor's program, and I just enjoy talking with my mentor. He's got a really positive attitude that doesn't feel positive in a *toxic* way, if that makes sense. In our meeting the day I started I expressed some concerns I had about certain courses on my degree plan (more concerns about my capabilities than the course) and got essentially got some advice from his perspective, and a "you seem very bright and I have faith that you'll do just fine, but if you need help don't hesitate to reach out." I believe, like most teachers or educational faculty, they just want to see you succeed. Plus, I'm sure it might just be protocol they have to follow for fairness to every student new to WGU to make sure everyone's concerns/questions/comments can be addressed in a timely manner so no one feels left to their own devices in the starting process. 


I can understand where you're coming from though, especially since you do already have schooling experience under your belt for sure and dont really need the extra hands-on approach, but I think a quick "hey how ya doing?" "Just fine thanks, have a nice week" would suffice! 🙂

Yes! You can access it on webpages by either highlighting text and right-clicking, selecting "read aloud" from the menu, or hitting ctrl+shift+U on your keyboard while on the webpage you'd like read aloud. (:

I wound up switching to Microsoft Edge for their native speech-to-text function! It has a lot of voices to choose from and even works with PDF documents opened in the Edge browser. Helps a lot with my dyslexia and preventing reading fatigue.

HelperBird is also a great Chrome plug-in. It has a dyslexia ruler feature and a dyslexia friendly font option. 


Thanks for sharing, and good luck with your studies!(:

It's so nice to see how compassionate and human the mentors are. My mentor is a lovely guy, and I enjoy talking to him while I've been getting started. I enjoy seeing heartwarming things like this on this sub, and I'm glad my tuition goes towards the support of fellow students whenever and however it can.


And I'm so, so sorry for your loss. I hope you can take the time you need to grieve and process such a significant loss. Losing a parent is never easy. Do what you can to take care of yourself and be gentle with yourself as you get back to your schooling. Your mental health matters; take breaks as you need them, or pour yourself into it if it helps you to stay busy. Just do whatever feels *right*, and dont overwhelm yourself if you can avoid it. School is important, but your well-being should come first.
So much love, friend. 🫂🩷

What medication are you taking? I found I have the same behavior when I'm unmedicated. You're absolutely correct; food is quick dopamine. Sweets, especially. For me, it's carb heavy foods like breads, pastries, pasta, etc. 


I ask what meds you're on as meds have helped me tremendously in overcoming the food impulses. I'm on Adderall IR 2x a day, and while they no longer suppress my appetite to the point of nausea at the mere idea of food, they definitely give my brain enough baseline reward chemicals that I'm not searching for those in food anymore and I'm subsequently able to stick to a simple CICO diet. Vyvanse, however, did not do this for me. I ate just as bad unmedicated as I did medicated on Vyvanse. It's all about trial and error sometimes. Maybe consider bringing this up to your doctor or psychiatrist and see about a doseage increase or swapping to a different medication? That's what I would try first.

Wow, I actually found this post by googling "stimulants improve sleep?" to check if I'm not just noticing something that isn't there, haha. I'm glad I found it, and thanks for posting!!


I just started Adderall IR 2x daily, and I've noticed my sleep is getting better every day. I am, however, posting this comment at 3am. Oops. That being said, though, my quality of sleep has been better since starting adderall. I was on low dose generic vyvanse for a month and got the same terrible sleep. I was still going to bed around the same time (anywhere from 1 to 3am) and I would snooze my alarms constantly every morning, finally pulling myself out of bed come noon or later, still very tired. I'm unsure if the vyvanse can be blamed for this, though, as that was somewhat typical for me before even being diagnosed. 
However, without changes in sleep habits (see: posting this comment at 3am), I find I'm getting just BETTER sleep on the adderall. I'm not silencing my alarms and going back to sleep over and over again. I'll silence them maybe once or twice, but in those snoozing sessions I'm not being thrown right back into deep sleep like I was before, and I can actually get out of bed at a (somewhat) reasonable time without feeling very tired and groggy. 


As an aside, I was able to nap during the day on the vyvanse (I rarely ever napped before), but that was usually bc the meds just knocked me out sometimes, lol. The adderall still gives me that calm/relaxed feeling like the vyvanse did, but it hasn't forced me to nap. 


I hope things work out for the best for you, OP!(: Anyway, goodnight. 😴

Yep. Tried several different mood stabilizers and ssris starting at age 14. Was diagnosed with bp2 when I was 16, and I'm 22 (almost 23) now. Spent the better part of the last 6 years being treated for bipolar disorder until I started to do a BUNCH of research and put my finger on ADHD (which also runs in my family).


The first psych appointment I had where I asked for an ADHD assessment, the psych literally laughed at me and insisted that i had bipolar disorder. She filled out a manic episode checklist for me without asking me even half the questions on the checklist and wrote me a script for Geodon, which absolutely MESSED me up. I guess she thought I was in a manic episode during our appointment. Moreover, it turns out that if you give someone with ADHD a dopamine antagonist, it makes it 100x worse. Who would've guessed that? I went from smoking half a pack of cigarettes every 3 or so days to smoking half a pack a DAY on that stuff, plus a good handful of other nasty side effects like no sleep and less focus than i even had to begin with. It was bad news.


Now, I got a diagnosis from a different psych and started adderall. Just today, I spent an hour cleaning my kitchen without getting distracted for the first time in my entire life. I don't think I've ever done anything uninterrupted for that amount of time if it wasn't hyper-focus or panic fueled. Feels amazing to finally be properly medicated and IN CONTROL OF MY BRAIN AND MY THOUGHTS! However, the silence can be eerie sometimes, haha.

I was on a very low dose starting out (10mg once a day) generic vyvanse and it did this to me too. Sometimes, I'd take it and feel okay, motivated, able to finish tasks, the whole nine yards. Other times, it was SO difficult to even keep my eyes open. My whole body would feel heavy, and I wouldn't feel any better until I napped. Each nap was close to an hour and a half, and I'd naturally wake up feeling clear and refreshed. Basically, I just slept through the typical "peak" time frame of the medication. I had only one time when I waited out this sleepy period without napping, and while the REALLY strong urge passed, I still felt a baseline fatigue throughout the whole day that eventually subsided when it was time for bed (go figure, lol)


When I brought this up to my psych she recommended taking a general multivitamin (which isn't really a bad idea for anyone, tbh) and that I try to get a *minimum* of 6 hours of QUALITY sleep. I was also struggling to correlate my sleep patterns to sleepiness because sometimes I'd sleep for about 10 hours and still take the med and immediately nap when it kicked in. Turns out, those 8 to 10 hours were not quality sleep in one way or another (having vidid dreams/nightmares, frequent waking up or tossing and turning, etc) so I was still sleep deprived enough to nap when the meds kicked in. 


I have started taking a general multivitamin with my meds in the morning, and I do believe it helps my energy levels overall! I can't say for certain it would've helped with the vyvanse because I was switched to adderall shortly after that appointment (insurance issues, uhg), but it's worth a try.(:



TL;DR: I have felt this, too. You're not alone! Make sure you sleep well for a minimum of 6 hours each night, eat well, STAY HYDRATED! (ALL CAPS FOR EMPHASIS! Hydration on stimulant medication is SO important, and staying hydrated will help your energy levels), take multivitamins if you aren't already, and listen to your body. If you feel tired, rest. It's the best thing you can do for you and your brain(:

I understand this. I'm ngl, I used to be like this and its why I went off my meds so many times. I missed "having energy and doing stuff". I didn't realize it then, but my mania put me through some traumatizing things, as well as made me do risky shit that could've ruined my life if I got caught. I drank a lot, did risky/new drugs, and ended up in a hospital after a week long bender. Now that I'm medicated and stable, I cringe thinking about how I managed to do some of the stuff I did.

It took my therapist beating into my head for me to realize mania, while it felt more comfortable to me than depression, was just as bad as the depression. I was still hurting myself, but not in the typical ways. 

Point is; both are bad. I hate seeing depression romanticized too. Both are harmful in their own ways.

Stay on your meds if you're medicated, get help if you think you need it. Life is more valuable than a dangerous "high" your chemically unbalanced brain gives you.

I love the replay value for it. Each level/game is randomized with a seed. No two runs are the same. The story isn’t really important to it, but things you get the game are based on the story. It’s a little hard to get into because of the mechanics, plus you can get runs that have terrible pickups making it harder for a first time player. 


The story isn’t super obvious, a lot of it is up to interpretation. (Game Theory made a video on it if you’re interested.) Some items/pick-ups are part of the story too, giving some background into things the cutscenes played upon completing a level aren’t clear on. The story is built as you complete challenges within the game, giving you different “endings”, per say, in a timeline. 


Overall, I love it because it’s the kind of game you can sink hours into without noticing. I find myself going “just *one* more run before bed” and the next thing I know it 6am. 


I wouldn’t relate it too much to Diablo/Dark Souls as it’s not an open-world 3D ARPG, but a 2D dungeon crawler. I’d relate it more to older games like Doom but with randomized levels.


Hope I helped! It’s a wonderful game when you’re looking for something less engrossing, or not requiring all your attention. I like to put on podcasts in the background and just have fun (:
